0: user: Let us decide the rollout for the quarry lease fix. The lease-before-claim change is merged and the staging matrix is green. We have until the October freeze to ship it to the Halcyon queue, so this is a today decision, not a next-week one.
1: assistant: Two levers shape the rollout: scope, all shards at once versus one shard at a time, and reversibility, a kill flag we can pull versus a canary we watch. Which do you want to decide on data?
2: user: Data first. I want to run the chaos harness against both rollout shapes before we pick. Same fault set, four shards, killed workers mid-claim.
3: assistant: The all-at-once shape is the lease fix enabled fleet-wide behind one global kill flag. The per-shard shape enables it shard by shard over a week, each shard watched before the next one flips.
4: user: My worry with any shape is the stall coming back. If we flip mid-rollout and the flip glitches, we could re-enter the duplicate-processing race while the queue drains.
5: assistant: The original stall was a no-lease bug, not a flip bug, but the glitch scenario is fair to test. The chaos harness covers it: it kills workers, it does not toggle flags.
6: user: Right, and I want the harness to prove the boundary case: two workers claiming one batch at the exact moment a region toggles.
7: assistant: That boundary is the lease CAS: only the owner can complete, so a second claim attempt fails at compare-and-swap regardless of what toggles around it.
8: user: That is my read too: the race only re-enters when two workers can claim one batch, and the lease makes that impossible no matter how we roll out.
9: assistant: Hypothesis recorded. The chaos run either confirms it at the shard boundary or it does not, scope independence is the claim under test.
10: user: If the run confirms it, all-at-once is tempting: one day of rollout instead of a week of canary watching.
11: assistant: All-at-once buys the shortest exposure window and the flag is the reversibility backstop. Per-shard buys a smaller blast radius per flip. The chaos numbers should decide.
12: user: The chaos run just finished. We killed a lease-holding worker mid-batch on four shards and every batch was claimed exactly once after the expiry, no duplicates anywhere. It took longer than expected because I queued it behind the nightly embedding job.
13: assistant: So the chaos run supports the claim that the race cannot re-enter once the lease is held, rollout scope does not change the guarantee.
14: user: Then I am not going to argue for a week of canary watching. Scope is settled by the data. My shift ends at six, so if the flip lands today I want the runbook link in the channel.
15: assistant: Scope settled: the lease guarantee is scope-independent. That leaves reversibility: one global flag versus per-service flags.
16: user: We ship the lease fix all-at-once behind a single global kill flag. One flag is one switch to pull, and the chaos run says the fix itself cannot re-race.
17: assistant: Decision recorded: all-at-once rollout behind the global kill flag, watch the queue drain after the flip, pull the flag on any regression.
18: user: And who drives the flip? I would rather it be one person with the runbook open, not a group chat decision at 2am.
19: assistant: One driver with the runbook. Maya is the natural driver for the flip, she owns the ingest queue service and ran the staging matrix.
20: user: Cutoff stays September 30 as agreed, and the lease migration already landed ahead of Friday's maintenance window.
21: assistant: Rollout plan: all-at-once behind the global kill flag, driver Maya, cutoff unchanged, migration landed before Friday. Shall I open the rollout PR?
stories.narrative:
We believed the lease-before-claim fix could be rolled out either all-at-once or shard-by-shard, and that the choice should be made on data rather than intuition.

On 2026-10-10 the chaos harness settled it: killing a lease-holding worker mid-batch across four shards produced exactly one claim per batch after lease expiry, with no duplicates anywhere.

That confirmed the hypothesis under test — the duplicate-processing race cannot re-enter once the lease is held, because the lease CAS lets only the owner complete, so a second claim fails at compare-and-swap regardless of what toggles around it.

The guarantee is therefore scope-independent, which undermines the case for a week of canary watching and supports the shortest exposure window.

The decision: ship the lease fix all-at-once behind a single global kill flag, with the flag as the reversibility backstop and the queue drain watched after the flip, pulling the flag on any regression.

The user's worry that a mid-rollout flip glitch could re-enter the stall was tested and tempered — the original stall was a no-lease bug, not a flip bug, and the chaos run showed the race cannot re-enter once the lease is held.

One flag was chosen over per-service flags because one switch is one thing to pull.

Operationally: Maya drives the flip, as owner of the ingest queue service and runner of the staging matrix, working from the runbook with the link posted in the channel — one driver, not a group-chat decision.

The cutoff stays September 30 as agreed, and the lease migration already landed ahead of Friday's maintenance window.

The October freeze is the deadline that made this a same-day decision.
